title: AN ELDERLY DAVID SHARED HIS BED WITH ABISHAG—YET SCRIPTURE SAYS HE DID NOT HAVE SEX WITH HER
paragraphs: AN ELDERLY DAVID SHARED HIS BED WITH ABISHAG—YET SCRIPTURE SAYS HE DID NOT HAVE SEX WITH HER

She was young. She was beautiful. She lay beside Israel’s aging king to keep him warm. But then Scripture inserts one deliberate sentence that changes how we must read the entire scene: “the king knew her not.” Why did God make sure we knew that?
There are Bible stories people sanitize because they feel uncomfortable.
And then there are Bible stories people sensationalize because uncomfortable details attract attention.
The story of David and Abishag deserves neither.
It deserves to be read exactly as Scripture gives it to us.

Because the opening chapter of 1 Kings brings us into a room where Israel’s legendary warrior-king is no longer standing over Goliath, fleeing Saul through the wilderness, dancing before the ark, commanding armies, or ruling from the strength of his throne.
David is old.
Very old.
And cold.
“So King David was old and advanced in years. And although they covered him with clothes, he could not get warm.” — 1 Kings 1:1
Pause there.
This is David.
The shepherd boy who faced a giant.
The fugitive who survived caves and spears.
The warrior whose name made enemies tremble.
The king who had experienced extraordinary victories and devastating failures.
The man who had tasted worship, warfare, friendship, betrayal, lust, adultery, murder, repentance, discipline, forgiveness, grief, and mercy.
Now he cannot even keep himself warm.
Time has reduced the warrior to an elderly man beneath blankets.
There is something painfully human about that.
Age eventually reaches the body that once seemed unstoppable.
Strength fades.
Hands that once carried weapons begin to tremble.
Eyes dim.
Bodies weaken.
Titles cannot stop mortality.
Money cannot command youth to return.
And even kings eventually discover that the human body does not bow to human authority.
David's servants therefore proposed a solution that sounds startling to modern readers:
“Let a young woman be sought for my lord the king, and let her wait on the king and be in his service. Let her lie in your arms, that my lord the king may be warm.” — 1 Kings 1:2
They searched throughout Israel.
Then they found her.
Abishag.
A young woman from Shunem.
Scripture does not hide her attractiveness:
“The young woman was very beautiful…”
And then comes the sentence that makes this story so easily misunderstood.
She attended the king.
She served him.
She lay with him as part of the effort to keep the elderly David warm.
Yet Scripture immediately tells us:
“…but the king knew her not.” — 1 Kings 1:4
The Hebrew is striking:
וְהַמֶּלֶךְ לֹא יְדָעָהּ
vehammelekh lo yeda‘ah
Literally, in context:
“And the king did not know her.”
The verb comes from יָדַע — yadaʿ, the ordinary Hebrew verb “to know.” But biblical Hebrew can also use “know” as a discreet expression for sexual relations.
Genesis gives us an unmistakable example:
“Now Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived…”
The connection between sexual union and conception makes the meaning clear.
So when 1 Kings deliberately tells us that David “did not know” Abishag, the narrator is telling us that despite their physical proximity, David did not have sexual relations with her.
That matters.
It means we should neither pretend the scene is less intimate than it is nor turn it into something Scripture explicitly says it was not.
Abishag was close enough to David to warm him.
She ministered to him.
She attended him.
She was beautiful.
She shared his bed.
And Scripture says:
He did not have sex with her.
Why does the Bible bother telling us?
The text itself does not stop and give us a theological essay explaining the narrator's reason, so we should be careful not to pretend God revealed motives that Scripture does not state.
But the detail becomes enormously important as the story continues.
Because David is dying.
And while an old king lies weak in bed, ambitious men are already thinking about the throne.
David's son Adonijah declares:
“I will be king.”
Suddenly 1 Kings 1 is no longer merely a story about an elderly man struggling to stay warm.
It is a succession crisis.
Power is moving.
Loyalties are being tested.
A throne is about to change hands.
Adonijah gathers supporters.
Nathan intervenes.
Bathsheba approaches David.
David reaffirms that Solomon is to succeed him.
Solomon is publicly anointed.
And the kingdom begins passing from David's hands into Solomon's.
Then David dies.
But Abishag's story is not over.
In 1 Kings 2, Adonijah approaches Bathsheba with a request.
He wants Abishag.
“Please ask King Solomon—he will not refuse you—to give me Abishag the Shunammite as my wife.” — 1 Kings 2:17
Solomon reacts with extraordinary seriousness.
“Ask for him the kingdom also…”
Why?
Whatever every cultural and political nuance behind Adonijah's request may have been, Solomon clearly understood it as having implications for the throne.
That means Abishag was not simply an irrelevant young woman inserted into the opening verses of Kings.
Her position in David's household became entangled with royal succession.
But there is another reason this opening scene hits so hard.
Because anyone who knows David's history knows exactly why seeing a beautiful young woman beside his bed immediately creates tension.
We remember Bathsheba.
We remember the rooftop.
We remember desire.
We remember adultery.
We remember Uriah.
We remember the attempted cover-up.
We remember blood.
We remember Nathan walking into the palace and confronting the king:
“You are the man!”
David's sexual history was not spotless.
Not even close.
The Bible refuses to airbrush its heroes.
That is one reason Scripture feels so brutally human.
David could write psalms and still sin sexually.
David could worship deeply and still make catastrophic decisions.
David could defeat Goliath publicly while losing another battle privately.
And maybe that is already touching somewhere you do not like being touched.
Because some of us have learned how to look victorious while secretly bleeding.
We know how to sing.
We know how to quote Scripture.
We know when to say “Amen.”
We know how to post the verse.
We know how to look faithful.
But there are rooms in the heart where Goliath was never the greatest enemy.
Lust was.
Pride was.
Bitterness was.
Pornography was.
Envy was.
Secret messages were.
An affair was.
An addiction was.
A hidden browser history was.
An unforgiving heart was.
A double life was.
Maybe everybody knows the version of you that killed the giant.
Very few know the version of you that stood on the rooftop.
That is why David's story is dangerous to reduce to either hero worship or scandal.
If all you see is the hero, you miss the warning.
If all you see is the scandal, you miss the grace.
David sinned terribly.
And when Nathan confronted him, David eventually stopped hiding behind royal power.
He said:
“I have sinned against the LORD.” — 2 Samuel 12:13
Those are only a few words.
But confession often begins when excuses finally die.
David could not undo what he had done.
Repentance did not resurrect Uriah.
Forgiveness did not magically erase every earthly consequence of David's actions.
Biblical grace is not God pretending sin did not matter.
Grace is costly precisely because sin does matter.
And this is where David's story begins pointing beyond David.
Because David was never the ultimate King.
Jesus is.
David needed mercy.
Jesus is the sinless Son of David who came bringing mercy.
David shed innocent blood.
Jesus willingly shed His own blood for sinners.
David's kingdom fractured.
Christ's kingdom will never end.
David failed.
Jesus did not.
David needed forgiveness.
Jesus purchased forgiveness for those who repent and trust in Him.
That is the Gospel.
Not:
“Try harder so God will finally love you.”
Not:
“Hide your scandal so religious people will respect you.”
Not:
“Your sin doesn't matter.”
And certainly not:
“You've sinned too badly, so there is no way home.”
The Gospel says that sin is so serious that the Son of God went to the cross—and grace is so astonishing that sinners can be forgiven through Him.
At Calvary, Jesus did not die for imaginary sinners with respectable imaginary sins.
He died for real sinners.
People with histories.
People with secrets.
People with regrets.
People who wish they could crawl backward through time and stop themselves from making that decision.
People who have cried afterward.
People who did it again afterward.
People ashamed to pray because they think heaven must be tired of hearing their apologies.
People who have wondered:
“After everything I've done, could Jesus possibly still want me?”
Listen carefully.
Your hope is not that your past becomes less sinful when enough years pass.
Your hope is Jesus Christ.
Your hope is not your ability to rewrite yesterday.
Your hope is the One who can redeem a life you cannot rewind.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9
That does not make repentance cheap.
It makes grace astonishing.
Real repentance does not say, “Jesus forgives me, so I'll keep feeding the sin that crucified Him.”
Grace teaches us to come into the light.
Grace calls us away from sin.
Grace restores us to God and begins changing us.
Maybe that is why this strange scene with an elderly David and Abishag is worth slowing down for.
We are seeing David near the end.
The body is weak.
The crown is about to pass to someone else.
His victories are behind him.
His failures are behind him too.
The giant is dead.
Uriah is dead.
Absalom is dead.
David's youth is dead.
And soon David himself will be dead.
But God's redemptive plan is not dead.
The story keeps moving.
David dies.
Solomon reigns.
Kings rise.
Kings fail.
The kingdom divides.
Prophets cry out.
Generations pass.
Empires rise and fall.
And eventually, in Bethlehem—the city of David—a Child is born.
Jesus.
The promised Son of David.
And suddenly we discover that the Bible was never ultimately asking us to place our hope in David.
David's life was always pointing beyond himself.
The warrior needed a greater Warrior.
The shepherd needed a greater Shepherd.
The king needed a greater King.
The sinner needed a Savior.
And so do we.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying something nobody knows.
Maybe there is a chapter in your story you would erase instantly if God gave you the chance.
Maybe you are exhausted from performing Christianity while quietly wondering whether Jesus could still receive the real you.
Stop hiding from the One who already knows.
Bring the sin into the light.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Run to Christ.
You do not need a better mask.
You need a Savior.
And His name is Jesus.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes a small act of honesty becomes the moment someone finally stops pretending.
Your testimony might become the sentence another wounded person desperately needs to read tonight.
We do not buy God's favor. We do not purchase grace. We give because grace has already been freely given to us in Christ.
Save what you may need again.
Follow so we can keep walking through Scripture together.
Pray that Jesus Christ—not Gospel Warrior, not a writer, not a platform—will be glorified through every person reached.
Because that is the point.
Not David.
Not Abishag.
Not scandal.
Not clicks.
Jesus.
The old king lying beside Abishag would eventually breathe his last.
But the King who came through David's line walked out of His tomb.
And that changes everything.
Your worst chapter does not need to become your final chapter.
Your hidden sin does not need to remain hidden.
Your shame does not need to become your identity.
Come into the light.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Follow Christ.
There is forgiveness at the cross.
There is cleansing in Christ.
There is a new life on the other side of surrender.
Because when Jesus takes hold of a surrendered life, the chapter you thought would bury you can become the place where grace begins writing something new.
